prompt: Why does `jina.py` need no Jina SDK to call Jina's embeddings endpoint?
hint: Compare the request and the answer with lesson 7's.

choices.text: Its request and answer copy the shape of OpenAI's /v1/embeddings
choices.why: Right. A POST with a bearer token, model and input in the body, data[i].embedding and usage in the answer: any HTTP client speaks that.

choices.text: Because labembed converts each request into Jina's own format first
choices.why: labembed answers the shape it receives; it converts nothing. Against api.jina.ai the same program works because Jina accepts that shape itself.

choices.text: httpx is Jina's official client library
choices.why: httpx is a general HTTP client that the openai package installed. Nothing about it is Jina's.

choices.text: Jina returns plain text, so there is nothing to decode
choices.why: Jina returns JSON with the vectors as lists of numbers, the same as OpenAI with encoding_format float.

prompt: `jina.py` printed `query and passage identical: True`. What does that line establish?
hint: Who computed the two vectors?

choices.text: That Jina's task field changes nothing in any model
choices.why: It shows nothing about Jina's models: no request reached Jina. jina-embeddings-v3 uses different weights per task, so its two vectors differ.

choices.text: Only that labembed ignores the task
choices.why: Right. Both lab models are symmetric: labembed checks and records the task and computes the same vector anyway. It is a fact about the lab, not about Jina.

choices.text: That retrieval.query and retrieval.passage are two names for one task
choices.why: Jina documents them as two tasks, one for the question and one for the text that answers it; that is the point of asymmetric search.

choices.text: That the second request was answered from a cache
choices.why: labembed computes every vector on every request; the log shows three separate successful requests.

prompt: A service logs "bad request, our bug" when an embedding call returns 400, and "provider outage, retry later" for any other error. What does it log when `task` is misspelled in a Jina call?
hint: Look at the status in the third line of jina.py's output.

choices.text: "bad request, our bug", since a misspelled field is a malformed request
choices.why: That would be right if the status were 400. Jina's refusal comes back as 422, which this check does not recognise.

choices.text: The outage message, and the call is repeated for nothing
choices.why: Right. The status is 422, so the check falls through to the outage branch, and repeating the call will not fix a wrong task name.

choices.text: Nothing, because Jina ignores fields it does not know
choices.why: That is labembed's behaviour for late_chunking, a field it does not implement. task is checked, and a bad value is refused.

choices.text: "bad request, our bug", because labembed answers 400 to every refusal
choices.why: labembed answered this one with 422; jina-log shows status 422 for the refused request.

prompt: What does Jina's `late_chunking` change, compared with embedding each chunk of a document on its own?
hint: Where does the cut between chunks happen, before the layers or after them?

choices.text: Each chunk is still embedded alone, only later, after the document is stored
choices.why: Late refers to where the cut happens inside the model, not to when the request is made.

choices.text: The whole document gets one vector, copied to every chunk
choices.why: Each chunk still gets its own vector; what changes is what the layers saw before the average.

choices.text: Chunks share the layers and split only at the average
choices.why: Right. Each chunk's vector is the mean of its own pieces, but those pieces were computed with the neighbouring chunks in view.

choices.text: The model decides where to cut the document
choices.why: The chunks are still yours, sent as the input list. The model only reads them together.

prompt: In a Jina request body, the field whose values include `retrieval.query` and `separation` is called ___.
hint: It tells the model what the text is for.

prompt: Match each Jina task to the text it is meant for.
hint: One description belongs to no task.

pairs.right: A help article a search should find
Two texts compared on an equal footing
Texts to be grouped into clusters

right_distractors: Detecting which language a text is in

prompt: `prices.py` prints `-` in the dims column for `voyage/voyage-3.5`. What does the dash mean?
hint: Whose sheet is it?

choices.text: voyage-3.5 returns vectors of no fixed length
choices.why: A model returns one dimension for every text; the dash says the sheet has no value, not that the model has none.

choices.text: The sheet records no dimension for it
choices.why: Right. A gap on a third party's sheet is a question for the provider's own documentation.

choices.text: The dimension is zero until a request asks for one
choices.why: Nothing on the sheet says so, and no model returns zero numbers by default.

choices.text: Voyage sells it only with the batch discount, which the sheet leaves out
choices.why: The batch column is a separate column, and it is also a dash. Neither dash says anything about how Voyage sells it.

prompt: `sheet.py` found 149 embedding rows, and the only row naming Jina has the mode `rerank`. What follows for this course?
hint: A reranker is not an embedding model.

choices.text: Jina's embedding models are free, which is why they have no price row
choices.why: A missing row is missing data, not a price of zero.

choices.text: Jina sells rerankers and no embedding models
choices.why: jina.py uses Jina's documented embeddings endpoint; the sheet simply does not list those models.

choices.text: It cannot quote a Jina embedding price from its one source
choices.why: Right. Every price here comes from LiteLLM's sheet at one commit, and that sheet has no Jina embedding row.

choices.text: Jina's embedding price is the reranker's price
choices.why: A reranker is a different model doing a different job; its price says nothing about embeddings.

prompt: Marginalia pays Together for `bge-base-en-v1.5` by the token. What does it keep that it would not keep with a model only its maker serves?
hint: Who else has the weights?

choices.text: The option of running the same open weights itself if it ever leaves the host
choices.why: Right. The weights are public, so the model does not depend on the host staying in business or keeping its price.

choices.text: A guarantee that the host's vectors match ones computed on its own machines
choices.why: That depends on whether the host runs the model at the same precision, and it is a question to ask before mixing them.

choices.text: Inputs of 32000 tokens
choices.why: That is Voyage's limit. The sheet lists 512 tokens for bge-base-en-v1.5.

choices.text: Customer texts that never leave its own servers
choices.why: A hosted model receives every text sent to it, whoever made the weights.

prompt: A model trained for one kind of text, such as `voyage-law-2` for contracts or `voyage-code-3` for programs, is called a ___ model.
hint: The word for a field of knowledge.

prompt: According to `static.py`, what is WordLlama's model?
hint: Look at the shape printed on the first line.

choices.text: Six transformer layers small enough to run on a CPU
choices.why: That describes MiniLM. WordLlama has no layers, which is what makes it static.

choices.text: A table of 32000 rows of 256 numbers
choices.why: Right. One row per token: a text's vector is the average of its tokens' rows, normalised, and the program rebuilt it by hand.

choices.text: A list of synonyms for each word
choices.why: No list of words is involved; the rows are numbers learned in training.

choices.text: An ONNX file like MiniLM's, five times smaller
choices.why: The file is a table of numbers in safetensors format, and there is no network in it to run.

prompt: In `misses.py`, WordLlama gave *Is there a cheaper postage option for a single paperback?* the label of a ticket about swapping a paperback for a hardcover. Why?
hint: What does an average of a dozen token vectors weigh?

choices.text: WordLlama saw more returns than shipping questions in training
choices.why: Nothing in the lesson measures its training mix, and the miss is explained by the words the two tickets share.

choices.text: The training ticket about the hardcover was mislabelled
choices.why: It is a returns question and is labelled returns; MiniLM found a different, shipping ticket.

choices.text: WordLlama cuts every text after its first few tokens
choices.why: It reads all the tokens; static.py averaged all 14 of this sentence's.

choices.text: A shared word weighs heavily in an average that ignores how words combine
choices.why: Right. paperback pulls both averages the same way, and with no layers nothing tells postage apart from swapping.

prompt: `speed.py` measured MiniLM at 723.6 ms for the 150 tickets. How many texts per second is that?
hint: Divide the texts by the seconds.

prompt: At the 26489 texts per second `speed.py` measured for WordLlama, how many seconds would 1,000,000 texts of that kind take on this machine?
hint: One million divided by the rate.

prompt: Put in order what `static.py` does by hand to rebuild WordLlama's vector for a sentence.
hint: The division by the length is last, as in every model this course runs.
items: Split the sentence into token ids
Take each token's row from the table
trap: Nothing runs between the lookup and the average: a layer there would make it a contextual model.

prompt: In `switch.py`, model B is model A rotated, and on its own it finds 19 of 24 right, like A. Why do B's questions against A's articles find 1?
hint: A rotation keeps the angles between B's vectors. What does it do to the coordinates?

choices.text: The rotation made B a worse model
choices.why: B scored 19 of 24 on its own, the same as A; a rotation changes no dot product within one model.

choices.text: Their coordinates mean different things
choices.why: Right. So a dot product between them measures nothing: the scores stay in a band of noise, from -0.151 to 0.210, with nothing standing out.

choices.text: The vectors lost their unit length in the rotation
choices.why: A rotation keeps every length; the trouble is the direction each coordinate now points in.

choices.text: Different dimensions, so NumPy mixed up the coordinates
choices.why: Both have 384 dimensions, which is why no error appeared. The ValueError came from WordLlama's 256.

prompt: During a migration, why keep writing to the old collection for a while after reads move to the new one?
hint: Think about the day something goes wrong with the new model.

choices.text: Queries are still compared against both collections and the scores merged
choices.why: That would mix two models in one ranking, which is the failure switch.py measured. Reads name one collection.

choices.text: The old model has to keep learning from new documents
choices.why: A model does not learn from the documents it embeds; its weights are fixed.

choices.text: So switching back is one change, with nothing missing
choices.why: Right. If the new model disappoints, the old collection is complete and current, and the search points back at it.

choices.text: Deleting a collection is only allowed once it receives no more writes
choices.why: Nothing forbids it; the reason is to keep the way back open, not a rule of the database.

prompt: The backfill step re-embeds 100,000 articles with MiniLM at the 207 texts per second `speed.py` measured. How many minutes does it take on this machine?
hint: Seconds first, then divide by 60.

prompt: Put the steps of moving a live search to a new model in order.
hint: Reads move only after the new collection is complete and measured.
items: Create a new collection and write every new document to both
Re-embed the existing documents into the new collection
Measure the new collection on the relevance judgements
Point the search at the new collection
trap: Backfilling before dual-writing leaves a gap: documents written during the backfill would be missing from the new collection.

prompt: The fact to store beside every vector, so that a query is only ever compared with vectors it can be compared with, is which ___ produced it.
hint: Name and version.

prompt: Jina publishes the weights of jina-embeddings-v3 under CC BY-NC 4.0. What does that mean for Marginalia, a shop?
hint: NC stands for non-commercial.

choices.text: Any open weights are free to run in production
choices.why: Open weights are a download, not a licence to use; the licence is a separate question and here it says non-commercial.

choices.text: Testing is fine, but production needs an agreement with Jina or its API
choices.why: Right. A non-commercial licence rules out running the weights in the shop's product without a separate agreement.

choices.text: The vectors it produces belong to Jina and cannot be stored
choices.why: The licence governs the weights, not the vectors you compute; the problem is running the model commercially at all.

choices.text: Only the code is restricted; the weights are MIT like WordLlama's
choices.why: It is the other way round in the lesson's example: the licence named is the weights'. WordLlama's package declares MIT.

prompt: A leaderboard ranks model X above model Y on average. On Marginalia's 24 questions, Y finds one more right article first than X. What is the sound conclusion?
hint: How much is one question out of 24 worth?

choices.text: Y is better for Marginalia, because its own data decides
choices.why: Its own data does decide, but one question in 24 is within noise; it needs more judgements or a look at the failures.

choices.text: X is better, because the leaderboard averages far more data
choices.why: More data, but not Marginalia's; WordLlama and MiniLM swapped places between two of the course's own tasks.

choices.text: One question in 24 separates nothing yet
choices.why: Right. Twenty-four questions catch a model that is clearly wrong, not a difference of one: add judgements and read the misses, which say more than the count.

choices.text: Pick the cheaper of the two, since quality is a tie
choices.why: Price comes last, after the measurement has said something; here it has not yet.

prompt: A marketplace must find near-duplicate listings among 50 million short product titles every night, on CPU servers. What is the reasonable first model to try?
hint: Short texts, a huge count, no GPU.

choices.text: A hosted transformer API, since only transformers compare short texts well
choices.why: WordLlama did as well or better than MiniLM on the short help-centre questions; and 50 million titles a night is a large bill and a lot of traffic.

choices.text: A static model, checked first on a sample of known duplicates
choices.why: Right. Short texts whose words carry the meaning are where an average holds up, and its speed fits the volume; the sample is what confirms it.

choices.text: MiniLM on one thread, as minilm.py runs it
choices.why: At the 207 texts a second measured here, 50 million titles take far longer than one night.

choices.text: Any model, because a job at night has no time limit
choices.why: It has to finish before the next night's run, and the measured speeds differ by two orders of magnitude.

prompt: A team swaps a 1536-dimension model for another 1536-dimension model, embeds only new articles with it, and keeps everything in one collection. What do they see?
hint: switch.py measured the case without an error.

choices.text: A dimension error on the first query
choices.why: The dimensions match, so the arithmetic runs; the ValueError in switch.py needed 256 against 384.

choices.text: Results and scores as usual, with the old articles ranked by pure noise
choices.why: Right. Nothing fails; new queries meet old vectors from another coordinate system, as B against A did in switch.py.

choices.text: The same ranking as before, because the dimension did not change
choices.why: The dimension is the count of numbers, not their meaning; two models' coordinates are unrelated.

choices.text: Old articles always ranking first, because they were stored earlier
choices.why: Storage order plays no part in a dot product; the old articles are ranked by noise, high or low.

prompt: Which of these are yes-or-no questions that rule a model out before anything is measured? Choose all that apply.
hint: A question with a measured answer belongs to the second pass.

choices.text: Is sending the texts to a hosted API allowed?
choices.why: Yes. If not, every hosted model is out, whatever it scores.

choices.text: Does the licence of the weights allow commercial use?
choices.why: Yes. A model you are not allowed to run is not worth measuring.

choices.text: Was it trained on the languages of the texts?
choices.why: Yes. Lesson 1 showed an English model treating a Portuguese title as unrelated to its translation.

choices.text: Does it find more right articles first on our 24 questions?
choices.why: That is the measurement of the second pass, made only on the models that survived the first.

choices.text: Is it the cheapest on the sheet?
choices.why: Price comes last, after the measurement; a cheap model that loses questions is not cheaper.
